text: Okay, so last part we left off asking what's actually going wrong inside these conversations. Let's open that up. Section 4.4 looks at interaction structure and content.
Structurally, are simulated and human conversations even comparable? Or is this apples to oranges from the start?

Surface level, they're pretty similar. Number of turns, number of actions, words per turn, all comparable between simulated and human user interactions. The differences show up when you look at content.
Content meaning what people actually say, not just how much of it.

Right. Take question-asking. Simulated user conversations include questions in 18.8% of user turns and 51.8% of agent turns. Human users only ask questions 9.8% of the time, though their agents ask questions more, 56.3%.
So simulated users are almost twice as curious as real ones. That's backwards from what I'd have guessed, real users navigating an unfamiliar agent should be the ones asking more.
And it's not uniform across human users either. Nigerian participants ask questions in only 4.3% of turns, well below the human average.
That's a real behavioral texture that a simulated user just isn't going to reproduce. What about politeness, please, thank you, apologizing, that kind of thing?

That gap is even bigger. Simulated conversations show politeness indicators in 39.2% of user turns and 52.0% of agent turns. Human conversations: 19.9% and 41.1%. And the paper's explicit that the simulated-versus-human gap is larger than any gap they see among different human subgroups.
So simulated users perform a kind of exaggerated politeness that doesn't track how any actual demographic talks to an agent. That's a specific, fixable-sounding miscalibration.
It is partially fixable, actually. They tried prompting simulated users to limit politeness, and that intervention did alter calibration patterns and shrink the gap for the most miscalibrated groups.

Good, so it's not hopeless, you can nudge the simulator toward realism if you know where to look. Let's get into the errors section, because that's the part I actually care about as an HCI person, what breaks and for whom.

They break errors into four types: argument errors, where the agent takes the right action with wrong arguments, missing action errors, extra action errors, and output errors, where the expected output is missing or wrong.
And do simulated and human conversations produce the same mix of those errors?
Not quite. Argument errors happen 32.2% of the time with simulated users, versus a range of 23.2% to 45.8% across human groups, with AAVE participants experiencing the highest rate.
That range across human groups alone is a fairness flag, before you even bring simulated users into it.
Agreed. But then missing and extra action errors actually run lower for simulated users: 17.8% versus 15.8% to 25.3% for missing actions, 5.6% versus 7.6% to 13.3% for extra actions.
So agents look more competent, more efficient, when they're talking to a simulated user.

Until you hit output errors, where the pattern flips. Agents omit or produce incorrect outputs 31.4% of the time with simulated users, compared to 12.2% to 23.6% for human users. That's the reverse direction from the action errors.

So agents act more cleanly with simulated users but talk back to them worse. That's a strange split, it's like the agent handles the mechanics fine but garbles the communication layer specifically for the fake user.
That's exactly their read too, agents behave differently with simulated versus human users. More complete, efficient action sequences, but more frequent output errors.
Okay, so who gets blamed when things go wrong, the agent or the user? That feels like the crux for anyone designing these systems.

This is where it gets sharp. Looking at manually annotated error attribution for failed tasks, agents are responsible for the failure 48.9% of the time in simulated conversations, versus only 24.5% in human conversations.
So in the simulated world, it's mostly the agent's fault. What's happening on the human side, then?

Users are the primary source of failure in human conversations, 62.2%, compared to 40% in simulated ones. There's also a small "both" and "other" category on each side, but that user-versus-agent flip is the headline.

That's a big deal for anyone reading simulated-user evals as a signal about agent quality. If real users are generating most of their own friction, error attribution and error mix, and this was manually annotated and matched on task difficulty, so it's not just noise, evaluating only on simulated users hides where the actual failures come from.
Which raises the obvious next question. If we know all this is broken, what's the field actually supposed to do about it? That's next.
